results.title: Separation of the paths that ask for it
results.observed: journal and data both live on /var/lib/basewright
results.remediation: Give them separate filesystems if the workload warrants it. Sharing costs failure isolation and makes one path able to fill the other; it is supported, and this is the record that it was chosen rather than overlooked.

results.title: The package repository answers
results.observed: the host did not report whether it can reach exampledb
results.remediation: Reaching a repository is proved from the host, which happens when the facts are collected over SSH. Until then this is unanswered rather than assumed, and the first task of apply is where it would otherwise be discovered.

parameters.why: A quarter of memory is the standard starting point for a shared cache, and it is capped because past that point the operating system page cache is the better place for the memory: it can be reclaimed under pressure, and this cannot.

This is charged per sort or hash node, not per connection, and a single query can hold several at once. The division by two is the allowance for that. It is written above the rule it depends on deliberately: the order values are computed in comes from what they read, not from where they sit in this file.
A fixed, conservative default. Above four hundred the answer is a connection pooler rather than a larger number here, because the memory cost is paid per backend.

One worker per core is the most the machine can run without them queueing behind each other. Past sixteen the coordination costs more than the parallelism returns on most workloads, and past thirty-two it stops returning anything at all.
On solid state storage a random read costs very nearly what a sequential one does, and a planner told otherwise will avoid indexes it should be using.
Longer intervals mean less write amplification and a longer recovery after a crash. Five minutes is the point where most workloads stop noticing either.

tunables.name: vm.swappiness
tunables.why: An instance whose cache the kernel has swapped out pays for the memory twice: once to hold it and again to fault it back in. Ten leaves the kernel room to swap under real pressure without doing it for the sake of the page cache.

tunables.name: vm.overcommit_memory
tunables.why: Refusing an allocation the machine cannot honour is better than granting it and having the out-of-memory killer choose which process dies, because it chooses the largest one, which is this instance.
